newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Counterfeiters thrive in low inflation Brazil.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Counterfeiters thrive in low inflation Brazil.

text.p: Brazil is suffering from a costly and unexpected side-effect of bringing hyper-inflation under control and creating a stable exchange rate for the first time in decades -- there's a boom in counterfeiting.
For the first time in recent memory, counterfeiting has become profitable and a booming underworld trade has attracted everyone from sophisticated forgers to small-time crooks.

"This is big business," said Antonio Carlos Meda, who heads the fight against counterfeiting at Brazil's Central Bank. "Inflation used to be a great ally of ours. Every time we printed a new note it was worth a lot less so quickly that there was no incentive to counterfeit," Meda explained.
With inflation at an almost-respectable 10 percent a year -- down from 2,700 percent in 1993 -- Brazil's criminals have discovered that counterfeiting pays.
Although the crime is difficult to measure, authorities say the $13.5 million in false bills seized last year is just a fraction of the amount in circulation.

Police say the sophistication of each operation varies widely in what remains a budding industry. Jailers once caught a talented inmate making remarkably good copies of bills by hand with a prison-issue easel and paint.

Aiding the illicit practice is the fact that it is not too difficult to counterfeit Brazil's reais currency, which was issued in July 1994 when the nation launched its landmark anti-inflation drive known as the Real Plan.
COUNTERFEITING BRAZILIAN MONEY EASY TO LEARN
Water marks and paper width on 50 reais and 100 reais bills, roughly equivalent in value to the $50 and $100 bill, are identical to those used for one, five and 10 reais notes.

Also, ink used on all the notes can be washed off without too much effort and the colours are easy to reproduce. This has allowed small-time counterfeiters to turn one reais notes into 100 reais notes with a little washing, tracing and colouring.

Up to now, Central Bank efforts to deter the crime have centred on training police and cashiers to detect fake bills. But the problem is growing so rapidly that the Central Bank has decided to change some physical aspects of the currency.
The bank hopes this year to begin printing one, five and 10 reais bills on thinner paper. These lower-denominated bills will carry different water marks from those on 50 and 100 reais bills.
The bank is also working on a major overhaul of its serial numbering system on bills, which should be ready by 2000.

"The basic principle is that economic stability is here to stay so we have to develop a new programme to inhibit counterfeiters," said Meda, who added he could not recall when counterfeiting was a serious problem in Brazil.
One reason the crime has grown so fast is that Brazilian authorities were not prepared to deal with the criminal consequences of having a currency worth counterfeiting.

Inflation, now at its lowest levels in almost 50 years, had been a problem in Brazil since the 1970s. Between 1986 and 1994, the nation went through a half dozen currencies, each of whose value was quickly eroded by hyper-inflation.

A foreign businessman living in Brazil during the late 1980s once returned to his apartment to find that thieves had made off with his television, stereo and other appliances, but left hundreds of dollars in various U.S. notes scattered on the floor.
"They were probably just kids who didn't recognise the money and thought it was an old, worthless currency," he said.
